en: The Rudrahṛdayopaniṣad: That Brahman which is revealed by the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) of the Heart of Rudra— that state of abiding as Brahman alone, I now worship.
Oṃ. May He protect us both together; may He nourish us both together; may we work together with great vigor.
May our study be radiant; may we never harbor hatred toward one another.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Hariḥ Oṃ.
The Heart [Upaniṣad], the Kuṇḍalī, the vision of the ashes and the multitude of Rudrākṣas, the Essence of the Praṇava, the Great Sayings (Mahāvākyas), and the Five Brahmans’ Agnihotra. || 1 ||
Having bowed his head at the feet of Vyāsa, Śuka said:
"Who is the god among all gods, and in whom do all the gods reside in every way? (2)
"By serving whom do the gods always remain pleased with me?
Having heard those words of his, the father replied to Śuka: (3)
Rudra is the essence of all the gods, and all the gods have Śiva as their essence.
On the right side of Rudra are the Sun, Brahmā, and the three fires.
On the left side are the goddess Umā, Viṣṇu, and Soma—these three.
She who is Umā is herself Viṣṇu, and he who is Viṣṇu is indeed the Moon.
Those who bow down to Govinda, they bow down to Śaṅkara;
those who worship Hari with devotion, they worship the bull-bannered Lord.
Those who hate Virūpākṣa hate Janārdana;
those who do not recognize Rudra do not know Keśava.
From Rudra the seed proceeds; Janārdana is the source of that seed.
He who is Rudra is himself Brahmā; he who is Brahmā is the consumer of oblations (Agni). || 8 ||
The universe consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, and of Agni and Soma;
everything that is masculine is Īśāna, and the feminine is the Blessed Umā.
All beings, whether born from eggs or otherwise, whether stationary or moving, consist of Umā and Rudra;
everything manifest is the form of Umā, while the unmanifest is Maheśvara.
The union of Umā and Śaṅkara is said to be Viṣṇu;
he who, endowed with devotion, should offer salutation to Him. (11)
Having understood the self as threefold—the individual self, the supreme self, and the inner self—one should take refuge in the supreme self. || 12 ||
The inner self is Brahmā, the supreme self is Maheśvara;
Viṣṇu is the eternal self of all beings indeed. || 13 ||
Of this tree of the three worlds, which has its branches and shoots rooted in the earth,
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Maheśvara are the tip, the middle, and the root respectively.
Viṣṇu is the effect, Brahmā is the action, and Maheśvara is the cause;
for the sake of a specific purpose, the single form was made threefold by Rudra.
Dharma is Rudra, Viṣṇu is the world, and the Grandfather is all-knowledge;
he who is wise should utter "Śrīrudra, Rudra, Rudra. (16)
By chanting the praises of the All-God, one is liberated from all sins;
Rudra is the man and Umā is the woman—to him and to her, salutations again and again. || 17 ||
Rudra is Brahmā and Umā is Vāṇī; salutations, repeated salutations to him and to her. Rudra is Viṣṇu and Umā is Lakṣmī; salutations, repeated salutations to him and to her. || 18 ||
Rudra is Sūrya and Umā is Chāyā; salutation, salutation to him and to her! Rudra is Soma and Umā is Tārā; salutation, salutation to him and to her! || 19 ||
Rudra is day and Umā is night; salutation, salutation to him and to her! Rudra is the sacrifice and Umā is the altar; salutation, salutation to him and to her! (20)
Rudra is fire and Umā is Svāhā; salutation, salutation to him and to her! Rudra is the Veda and Umā is the teaching; salutation, salutation to him and to her! || 21 ||
Rudra is the tree and Umā is the creeper; salutations, salutations to him and to her. Rudra is the fragrance and Umā is the flower; salutations, salutations to him and to her. || 22 ||
Rudra is the object and Umā is the imperishable; salutations, repeated salutations to him and to her!
Rudra is the *liṅga* and Umā is the pedestal; salutations, repeated salutations to him and to her! || 23 ||
One should pay homage individually to Rudra, who embodies all the gods;
with these very words of mantra, one should bow to Īśa and Pārvatī.
Wherever one may be, if one should recite this mantra together [with the image], even a killer of a Brahmin is liberated from all sins while standing in the midst of water. || 25 ||
The supreme, eternal Brahman is the foundation of all, free from duality, whose nature is existence,
consciousness, and bliss, and which transcends the reach of speech and mind.
O Śuka, when that is well known, all this becomes known;
for everything has that as its essence, and therefore nothing exists anywhere as distinct from it.
Indeed, two kinds of knowledge are to be known: the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā). Of these, this lower knowledge consists of the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda. (28)
Likewise, O Lord of Sages, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda, phonetics (śikṣā), ritual manuals (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), and prosody (chandas). || 29 ||
And just as the science of astrology [is not the self], so too the cognitions do not have the self as their object;
yet this is the supreme knowledge by which the self is known as the supreme imperishable.
That which is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, and devoid of form;
that which is beyond the reach of eyes and ears, and likewise without hands or feet—31.
The wise behold that eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, extremely subtle, and imperishable Self— the source of all beings— within their own selves.
He who is all-knowing and all-wise, whose austerity consists of knowledge—
from Him the succession of worlds is born here in the form of food.
All that appears as real exists like a snake in a rope;
this imperishable reality is the truth, and by realizing it, one is liberated. || 34 ||
For indeed, the destruction of saṃsāra occurs through knowledge alone, and not through ritual action.
One should approach one's own guru—who is learned in the Vedas and established in Brahman—in accordance with the prescribed rule.
The guru should impart the supreme knowledge that awakens one to the Self as Brahman to that person,
provided he knows the Imperishable One which is directly hidden in the cave of the heart.
Having severed the great knot of ignorance, one shall go to the eternal Śiva;
this is the immortal truth, which must be understood by those seeking liberation. 37.
The bow is the Om (Tāra), the arrow is indeed the Self (Ātman), and Brahman is said to be the target.
One should pierce it with undistracted mind; like the arrow, one should become absorbed in That. 38.
The target is indeed all-pervading, and the arrow is all-pervading;
the archer is also all-pervading—the target of Śiva is beyond doubt. (39)
There the radiance of the sun and moon does not shine,
nor do the winds blow, nor do all the deities;
this is that very god who has become the very essence of existence.
Being himself pure and free from passion, he shines forth. || 40 ||
In this body, two birds—the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśa)—dwell together as companions. Of these two, the individual soul enjoys the fruit of its actions, but not the Great Lord.
Maheśvara shines forth by himself solely in the form of a witness, devoid of enjoyment; the distinction between these two is merely imagined through Māyā. 42.
Just as the space within a jar and the space within a hut are conceptualized as divisions of space,
so too are the supreme [realities] conceptualized in the forms of the individual soul (jīva) and Śiva.

In reality, Śiva is directly consciousness itself, and the individual soul is always so by its own nature; they are distinct in the form of consciousness and non-consciousness, yet not distinct, for that would entail the loss of their essential nature as consciousness.
The consciousness of consciousness does not differ from the form of consciousness because of its insentient nature;
if it were to differ, that difference would be insentient, whereas consciousness alone is indeed always one. (45)

Because the oneness of consciousness is established both through reasoning and through valid means of knowledge, one who thoroughly realizes this oneness of consciousness neither grieves nor is deluded. (46)
He indeed attains non-duality, supreme bliss, auspiciousness, and absolute liberation. || 47 ||
Having ascertained, "I am that which is the support of the entire universe, the mass of reality and consciousness," the sage becomes free from sorrow. (48)
Those whose defects have been extinguished perceive within their own bodies the Self, which is of the nature of self-luminous light and the witness of all; others, veiled by *māyā*, do not.
Thus, for that supreme yogin who possesses full comprehension of form, there is no going anywhere, as he is one whose true nature is complete. (50)
Just as the one, all-pervading space does not go anywhere, so too the knower of the Self does not go anywhere. 51.
The sage who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself—established in its own nature, having existence, consciousness, and bliss as its constituent essence. || 52 ||
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
Oṃ. May He protect us both together; may He nourish us both together; may we work together with great vigor.
May our study be radiant; may we never harbor mutual hatred.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Thus ends the Rudrahṛdaya Upaniṣad.
